parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian абориге́н (aborigén), from Latin aborīginēs, a formation of ab + orīgine, literally “from the beginning”.

parole.significato: abrasive (substance used for cleaning, smoothing, or polishing)
parole.testo: Probably borrowed from Russian абрази́в (abrazív), from French abrasif.

parole.significato: absolute (concentrated natural flower oil, used for perfumes; an alcoholic extract of a concrete)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian абсолю́т (absoljút), through Latin absolutus (“unconditional; unfettered; completed”).
Borrowed from Russian абсолю́тный (absoljútnyj), ultimately from Latin absolūtus (“unrestricted, unconditional”).

parole.significato: to absolutize (to treat as the most important or logical)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian абсолютизи́ровать (absoljutizírovatʹ). By surface analysis, абсолю́т (absoljút) + -изи́рам (-izíram).

parole.significato: absolutism (belief in a metaphysical absolute; belief in Absolute)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian абсолюти́зм (absoljutízm).
Borrowed from Russian абстра́ктный (abstráktnyj) and German abstrakt, both borrowed from Latin abstractus (“drawn away from”).
Borrowed from Russian абстраги́ровать (abstragírovatʹ) and German abstrahieren, both from Latin abstrahō.

parole.significato: outport (the outer or front part of a harbour protected by a breakwater, where ships anchor and where loading and unloa…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian аванпо́рт (avanpórt), from French avant-port.

parole.significato: male adventurer, male venturer, male swashbuckler
parole.testo: From Russian авантюри́ст (avantjuríst), from French aventuriste or aventurier. By surface analysis, авантю́ра (avantjúra, “adventure”) + -ист (-ist, “-ist, -er”).

parole.significato: augur, soothsayer (diviner who foretells events by unusual occurrences)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian авгу́р (avgúr), ultimately from Latin augur.

Borrowed from Russian августе́йший (avgustéjšij), a partial calque of Latin augustissimus. Suffixed with the Slavic superlative suffix -ейши (-ejši) (Russian -ейший (-ejšij)), corresponding to Latin -issimus.

parole.significato: aeronautics (the science of the movement of aircraft)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian авиа́тика (aviátika), from German Aviatik.

parole.significato: submachine gunner; machine gunner, tommy gunner
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian автома́тчик (avtomátčik). Equivalent to автома́т (avtomát) + -чик (-čik).
Borrowed from Russian авториза́ция (avtorizácija) and French autorisation, from Medieval Latin auctōrizātiō.
Borrowed from Russian авторитарный (avtoritarnyj), from French autoritaire.

parole.significato: authoritarianism (a system of political governance based on complete subordination of the individual to state authority)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian авторитаризм (avtoritarizm) from French autoritarisme.

parole.significato: authority, prestige (the power to influence or command thought, opinion, or behaviour)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian авторите́т (avtoritét), German Autorität, and French autorité, ultimately from Latin auctōritās.

parole.significato: male agent, male factor (one who acts in place of another)
parole.testo: From Russian аге́нт (agént) and German Agent, from Latin agēns (genitive agentis).

parole.significato: intelligence agency; an agency that serves to further some other entity's interests and ideas
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian агенту́ра (agentúra), from German Agentur.
From Russian агита́тор (agitátor) and German Agitator, from Latin agitātor (“charioteer, drover”).

parole.significato: to canvass (solicit votes in a political campaign)
parole.testo: Via Russian агити́ровать (agitírovatʹ) and German agitieren from Latin agitō. See also агита́тор (agitátor).
From Russian аги́тка (agítka), ostensibly abbreviated Latin agitātiō + -ка (-ka). Akin to агитпу́нкт (agitpúnkt), Russian агитпро́п (agitpróp, “agitprop”), etc.
Borrowed from Russian агитпро́п (agitpróp) — see Russian section below for further details.
Borrowed from Russian агитпу́нкт (agitpúnkt), ultimately from abbreviated Latin agitātiō + pūnctum.
Borrowed from Russian аго́ния (agónija) and Polish agonia, in turn from Ancient Greek ἀγωνία (agōnía, “emulation, competition, struggle”).
Via Russian агра́рный (agrárnyj) and German agrarisch, from Latin agrārius, derived from ager (“field”).
Borrowed from Russian агрега́т (agregát) and German Aggregat, from Latin aggregātus from the verb aggregō (“bring, attach”).

parole.significato: aggression (act of invasion, militant force, etc.)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian агре́ссия (agréssija) and German Aggression, ultimately from Latin aggressiō.
Borrowed from Russian агре́ссор (agréssor) and German Aggressor.
Via Russian агроно́м (agronóm), from Latin agronomus, from Ancient Greek ἀγρονόμος (agronómos, “agricultural overseer”). Its entry into Bulgarian was further influenced by French agronomie.

parole.significato: adaptation, adaption, adjustment (the quality of being adapted)
parole.testo: Internationalism, from Russian адапта́ция (adaptácija) & German Adaption, ultimately from Medieval Latin adaptātiō, from Latin adaptāre (“to adjust, fit”).
Borrowed from Russian администра́тор (administrátor) and German Administrator, both from Latin administrātor.
Borrowed from Russian администра́ция (administrácija) and German Administration, from Latin administrō, administrātiō.

parole.significato: admiralty (of or pertaining to an admiralty)
parole.testo: Ostensibly, адмиралте́йство (admiraltéjstvo) + -ски (-ski), replacing the -ство (-stvo, “-hood”) suffix with -ски (-ski, “-ic”, relational adjective suffix). адмиралте́йство (admiraltéjstvo) is originally a borrowing from Russian, in turn from Dutch, so one could also analyze this term as Dutch admi

parole.significato: admiralty (office or jurisdiction of an admiral)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian адмиралте́йство (admiraltéjstvo).

parole.significato: sender, consignor, shipper (someone who addresses something to someone else)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian адреса́нт (adresánt), from French adressant.

parole.significato: adjutant (lower-ranking military serviceman who helps his senior)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian адъюта́нт (adʺjutánt) and German Adjutant, from Latin adiūtō, frequentative of adiuvō (“assist”).
Borrowed from Russian азо́т (azót), from French azote (coined by French nobleman and chemist Antoine Lavoisier), ultimately from Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “not”) + ζωή (zōḗ, “life”).
Possibly borrowed from Russian азо́тистый (azótistyj).
From Russian ака́ция (akácija) and German Akazie, from Latin acacia and Ancient Greek ἀκακία (akakía).
From Russian акваре́ль (akvarélʹ) or German Aquarell, from French aquarelle and Italian acquerello, ultimately from Latin aqua.
From Russian акклама́ция (akklamácija) and German Akklamation, from Latin acclāmatiō.
From Russian акселера́ция (akselerácija) and German Akzeleration, from Latin accelerātiō.
From Russian аксио́ма (aksióma), German Axiom, and French axiome, from Latin axiōma, in turn from Ancient Greek ἀξίωμα (axíōma).
Borrowed from Russian аксиомати́чный (aksiomatíčnyj). By surface analysis, аксио́ма (aksióma) + -и́чен (-íčen, adjectival suffix).

parole.significato: male activist, male militant, male active member of an organization
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian активи́ст (aktivíst).

parole.significato: topical, current, of the day, pressing
parole.testo: From Russian актуальный (aktualʹnyj), from Latin āctuālis.
Borrowed from Russian аку́ла (akúla), borrowed from a Sami language, borrowed from Old Norse hákarl, from hár (“shark”) + karl (“man”).
From Russian акуше́р (akušér), from French accoucheur.
Borrowed from Russian акцентуа́ция (akcentuácija), from French accentuation.

parole.significato: excise, excise tax (any of various taxes levied on the production or sale of certain goods, especially on luxuries, tob…
parole.testo: From Russian акци́з (akcíz), German Akzise, and possibly French accise, from Late Latin accisum (“used up, consumed”), in reference to the tax being levied on consumable goods such as tobacco and alcohol. Ostensibly from Russian акционе́р (akcionér) or German Aktionär, in turn from or directly from French actionnaire.
Borrowed from Russian анархи́зм (anarxízm), from French anarchisme.
Borrowed from Russian анархи́ст (anarxíst), borrowed from French anarchiste, from anarchie (“anarchy”) + -iste.
Borrowed from Russian антра́кт (antrákt), in turn from French entracte.
Borrowed from Russian ао́рист (aórist), in turn from Ancient Greek ἀόριστος (aóristos, “not done, not completed”).
Borrowed from Russian апоге́й (apogéj), а transliteration of Ancient Greek ἀπόγειον (apógeion, “far from the earth”).
Borrowed from Russian апте́ка (aptéka), from Ancient Greek ἀποθήκη (apothḗkē).
Probably borrowed from Russian армату́ра (armatúra), from Latin armātūra (“weapons”).
Borrowed from Russian армейский (armejskij).
Borrowed from Russian арти́кул (artíkul), from Latin articulus.
Probably borrowed from Russian арти́ст (artíst), from French artiste.

parole.significato: association (a group of persons associated for a common purpose)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian ассоциация (associacija) and German Assoziation.
Borrowed from Russian атама́н (atamán) via a Turkic language.
Via Russian афе́ра (aféra) from French affaire.
Borrowed from Russian бак (bak), from Dutch bakboord.
Borrowed from Russian балл (ball), borrowed from French balle.
Borrowed from Russian бала́нс (baláns), from French balance. First attested in 1857.
Borrowed from Russian бамбу́к (bambúk), from Portuguese bambu, from Malay bambu.
Borrowed from Russian ба́нда (bánda), German Bande, or French bande.
Borrowed from Russian ба́нка (bánka).

parole.significato: shoulder, banquette, wayside (strip of land on both sides of a road surface)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian банке́т (bankét).

Borrowed from Russian бард (bard), borrowed from English bard, from Scottish Gaelic bàrd, from Old Irish bard, from Proto-Celtic *bardos, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷerH-dʰh₁o-, from *gʷerH- + *dʰeh₁-.
Borrowed from Russian барда́к (bardák).
Borrowed from Russian баро́н (barón) or French baron, from Medieval Latin bārōnis, from Frankish *barō or another Germanic language. First attested in 1762.
Borrowed from Russian барс (bars), From a Turkic language, ultimately from Proto-Turkic *bars, also related to Proto-Mongolic *bars. See Turkish pars, Mongolian бар (bar), Dongxiang basi.
Borrowed from Russian бастион (bastion), from French bastion.
Borrowed from Russian батаре́я (bataréja), from French batterie.
Borrowed from Russian бегемо́т (begemót).
Borrowed from Russian бе́дствие (bédstvije). By surface analysis, беда́ (bedá, “trouble”) + -ствие (-stvie).
Borrowed from Russian бе́жевый (béževyj), ultimately from French beige.
Borrowed from Russian беспе́чный (bespéčnyj).
Borrowed from Russian беспорядок (besporjadok).
Borrowed from Russian белу́га (belúga). Morphologically parsable as бял (bjal, “white”) + -уга (-uga).
Borrowed from Russian бельё (belʹjó).

parole.significato: a person who had a high social status in the past due to wealth or power
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian бы́вший (bývšij).
Borrowed from Russian бизон (bizon) or French bison, from Latin bisōn, from Proto-Germanic *wisundaz.
Borrowed from Russian бинт (bint), from German Binde.

parole.significato: beingness, existence, state of being (the quality or condition of being or existing)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian бытность (bytnostʹ).

parole.significato: spoon lure, spinner (type of fishing lure)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian блесна́ (blesná).

parole.significato: dish, plate, platter (a flat or shallow vessel used for serving or holding food)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian блю́до (bljúdo), from Proto-Slavic *bľudo.

parole.significato: bogatyr, medieval heroic warrior in Kievan Rus
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian богаты́рь (bogatýrʹ).

parole.significato: lively, fresh, alert, buoyant, jaunty, spry, cheerful, jolly
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian бодрый (bodryj), from Proto-Slavic *bъdrъ (“alert, cheerful”).
Borrowed from Russian большеви́к (bolʹševík).
Borrowed from Russian бра́га (brága).

parole.significato: canvas (coarse waterproof fabric for covering objects left outdoors)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian брезе́нт (brezént), from презенинг (prezening, earlier form), borrowed from Dutch presenning, possibly borrowed from Portuguese percinta, from Latin praecingō, from prae- + cingō.

parole.significato: breeze (either land breeze or sea breeze)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian бриз (briz), from French brise.

parole.significato: unrest, ferment, agitation (public manifestation of discontent)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian броже́ние (brožénije).

parole.significato: armour (UK), armor (US) (protective layer over a body, vehicle, or other object intended to deflect or diffuse damage)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian броня́ (bronjá). Displaced native бръня (brănja), from Proto-Slavic *brъňa, of Gothic origin.
Possibly borrowed from Russian бу́лка (búlka).

parole.significato: den, lair, burrow (the dwelling or hiding place of a wild animal)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian берло́га (berlóga), from Proto-Slavic *bьrloga.
Borrowed from Russian бюдже́т (bjudžét), derived from English budget. First attested in 1871.

parole.significato: important (having relevant and crucial value), of importance, momentous, crucial, key, grave, weighty, substantial, mat…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian ва́жный (vážnyj). Ultimately from Polish ważny.
Borrowed from Russian ва́за (váza), borrowed from French vase.
Borrowed from Russian валидо́л (validól).
Borrowed from Russian ведо́мый (vedómyj, “driven”). Equivalent to the lost present passive (perfective) participle of веда́ (vedá, “to conduct”) + -ом (-om), from Proto-Slavic *vesti.
Borrowed from Russian ве́жливый (véžlivyj).
Borrowed from Russian вежли́вость (vežlívostʹ). By surface analysis, вежли́в (vežlív, “courteous, polite”) + -ост (-ost, “-ness”).

parole.significato: omnipresent, ubiquitous, all-present (present everywhere; existing or appearing in all places)
parole.testo: Partial calque of Russian вездесу́щий (vezdesúščij). By surface analysis, Russian везде (vezde) + Bulgarian същ (săšt).

parole.significato: Majesty (referring to a king or queen)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian вели́чество (velíčestvo), from Old Church Slavonic величьство (veličĭstvo). By surface analysis, вели́к (velík) + -ество (-estvo)
Borrowed from Russian вели́чие (velíčije), from Old Church Slavonic величьѥ (veličĭje). By surface analysis, вели́к (velík) + -ие (-ie).

parole.significato: probable, likely, contingent, on the cards, in the cards
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian вероя́тный (verojátnyj).
Borrowed from Russian вероя́тность (verojátnostʹ), instead of expected вероетност (veroetnost).
Borrowed from Russian вертолёт (vertoljót). Cognate with the native въртолет.
Borrowed from Russian вещево́й (veščevój).
Borrowed from Russian взаимоде́йствие (vzaimodéjstvije).
Borrowed from Russian взвод (vzvod).

parole.significato: break-in, forced entry (entry into a building, room, safe, vehicle, or other closed place by breaking or forcing a lock…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian взлом (vzlom).

parole.significato: gaze, look, glance (the act or direction of looking; a poetic word for one’s look or gaze)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian взор (vzor), from Proto-Slavic *vъzorъ.
Borrowed from Russian взрыв (vzryv).

parole.significato: class (collection of students at the same level of eduction)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian вы́пуск (výpusk). Synchronically analyzable as ви- (vi-) + *пу́ск (*púsk, “release”).
Borrowed from Russian вы́стрел (výstrel). Synchronically analyzable as ви- (vi-) + стрел (strel, “shooting”).

An old ī-stem agent noun borrowed from Russian вити́я (vitíja), ultimately from Old Church Slavonic вѣтии (větii), from Proto-Slavic *věti. Reanalyzed in Russian and whence Bulgarian with the suffix -ия (-ija).

parole.significato: influence (The power to affect, control or manipulate something or someone.)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian влия́ние (vlijánije).
Borrowed from Russian вменя́емый (vmenjájemyj). Formally a present passive participle вменя́я (vmenjája, “to impute, to put in one's mind”) + -яем (-jaem).

parole.significato: to implement, to introduce (new methods, technologies, etc.)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian внедрить (vnedritʹ).

parole.significato: vodka (a clear distilled alcoholic liquor made from grain mash)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian во́дка (vódka).
Borrowed from Russian водопрово́дчик (vodoprovódčik), morphologically equivalent to водопрово́д (vodoprovód, “plumbing, water conduit”) + -чик (-čik).
Borrowed from Russian водоросли (vodorosli).
Borrowed from Russian водоро́д (vodoród), a calque of French hydrogène, itself derived from Ancient Greek ὕδωρ (húdōr, “water”) + γεννάω (gennáō, “I bring forth”).
Borrowed from Russian вопль (voplʹ).
Borrowed from Russian впечатле́ние (vpečatlénije), itself a calque of the German Eindruck calqued from French impression.

parole.significato: however, though, nevertheless, still (used to introduce a qualification, reservation, or contrast to what has just been…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian впро́чем (vpróčem). Cognate with Bulgarian про́чее (próčee).
Calque of Russian вездехо́д (vezdexód). By surface analysis, всъде (vsăde) + ход (hod).

parole.significato: by all means, in any way
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian вся́чески (vsjáčeski). By surface analysis, всеки (vseki, “each”) + -ески (-eski).
Borrowed from Russian вулка́н (vulkán) or German Vulkan, from Latin Vulcānus (“Roman God of fire; a specific volcanic island”).
Borrowed from Russian углеро́д (ugleród).
Borrowed from Russian вожделе́ние (voždelénije), from Old Church Slavonic. By surface analysis, въз- (văz-) + жела́ние (želánie).

parole.significato: appeal, proclamation, address, call, manifesto (a public written or spoken appeal calling on people to act, support, re…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian воззва́ние (vozzvánije). By surface analysis, въз- (văz-) + звание (zvanie).

parole.significato: retribution, punishment, just deserts (punishment or repayment for a crime, evil, or wrongdoing)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian возме́здие (vozmézdije).
Borrowed from Russian возмуще́ние (vozmuščénije), from Old Church Slavonic възмѫщениѥ (vŭzmǫštenije).
Borrowed from Russian восто́рг (vostórg).

Borrowed from Russian вообще́ (voobščé). By surface analysis, въ (vă, “in”) + общ (obšt, “general, total”) + -е (-e, adverb-forming suffix), literally “in total, in the whole”. Formed with similar semantics to изо́бщо (izóbšto, literally “from the whole”).
Borrowed from Russian вопроси́тельный (voprosítelʹnyj).
Borrowed from Russian вопро́сник (voprósnik). By surface analysis, въпро́с (văprós) + -ник (-nik).

Borrowed from Russian геогра́фия (geográfija). By surface analysis, гео- (geo-) + -графия (-grafija).

Borrowed from Russian главнокомандующий (glavnokomandujuščij). By surface analysis, гла́вен (gláven) + -о- (-o-) + кома́ндващ (komándvašt).
Borrowed from Russian глаго́л (glagól), from Old Church Slavonic глаголъ (glagolŭ), from Proto-Slavic *golgolъ (“speech, word”). Ultimately a calque of Latin verbum.

parole.significato: furnace, forge, hearth (a furnace, hearth, or chamber in which metal, ore, fuel, or other material is heated, burned, m…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian горни́ло (gornílo), from Proto-Slavic *gъrnidlo.

parole.significato: lady (a polite term referring to a woman)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian госпожа́ (gospožá), displacing earlier Old Church Slavonic госпожда (gospožda) and Middle Bulgarian господжа (gospodža), utimately from Proto-Slavic *gospoďa.
Borrowed from Russian гравита́ция (gravitácija); ultimately from Latin grāvitās (“heaviness”).
Borrowed from Russian гравито́н (gravitón) or English graviton.

parole.significato: to rout, to crush, to destroy
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian громи́ть (gromítʹ), from Proto-Slavic *gromiti.
Borrowed from Russian гру́ппа (grúppa) (which from German Gruppe, in turn from the following French) and French groupe, from Italian gruppo.

parole.significato: emphasizes or highlights a point: even
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian даже (daže), from Proto-Slavic *da že.

parole.significato: data, facts, information, evidence, record, background
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian да́нные (dánnyje).
Borrowed from Russian да́тчик (dátčik). Morphologically equivalent to the diminutive of да́тък (dátăk, “giver, provider”) (dialectal) + -ик (-ik).
Borrowed from Russian двоето́чие (dvojetóčije).
Borrowed from Russian дворя́нин (dvorjánin). By surface analysis, двор (dvor, “courtyard”) + -янин (-janin).

Possibly borrowed from Russian мозо́ль (mozólʹ) or a reanalyzed form of an earlier мозо́л (mozól) (cognate to the Russian term).
Borrowed from Russian ма́монт (mámont).

parole.significato: manat (national unit of currency in Azerbaijan and Turkmenistan)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Azerbaijani and Turkmen манат (manat), both of which are from Russian моне́та (monéta).
Built on the basis of Russian маслобо́йня (maslobójnja); equivalent to Bulgarian масло (maslo, “butter”) + бой (boj, “beating”) + -на (-na).

parole.significato: continent (one of the largest continuous landmasses of the Earth, surrounded wholly or mostly by ocean)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian матери́к (materík).
Borrowed from Russian маши́на (mašína), borrowed from German Maschine, borrowed from French machine, from Middle French machine, borrowed from Latin māchina. First attested in 1842.
Borrowed from Russian ме́дик (médik), from Latin medicus. First attested in 1871.
Borrowed from Russian междоме́тие (meždométije).
Borrowed from Russian меланхо́лия (melanxólija), from Ancient Greek μελαγχολία (melankholía, “blackness of the bile”).

parole.significato: minuet (slow graceful dance consisting of a coupé, a high step, and a balance)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian менуэ́т (menuét), from French menuet.
Borrowed from Russian мерза́вец (merzávec). Мorphologically equivalent to ме́рзав (mérzav, “vile”) (obsolete) + -ец (-ec).

Borrowed from Russian ме́рзкий (mérzkij), formally reflecting Proto-Slavic *mьrzъkъ (“frosty, cold”) (probably originally meaning cold hearted). Related to Bulgarian мръ́зна (mrắzna, “to feel cold”) + -ък (-ăk).
Borrowed from Russian ме́ткий (métkij). By surface analysis, Proto-Slavic *mětiti (“to mark, to calculate”) + -ък (-ăk).

parole.significato: militsia, police (state administrative service for maintaining order and safety in Bulgaria between 1944 to 1990)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian мили́ция (milícija), from Latin militia.

parole.significato: while passing by, in passing (while going past or passing by something)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian мимохо́дом (mimoxódom).
Borrowed from Russian мини́стр (minístr) and French ministre, ultimately from Latin minister (“servant”).
Borrowed from Russian момента́льный (momentálʹnyj).

parole.significato: monument (structure built for commemorative or symbolic reasons)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian монуме́нт (monumént), from Latin monumentum. First attested in 1843.
Borrowed from Russian морж (morž).
Borrowed from Russian москви́ч (moskvíč).

parole.significato: small quay, pier (on a river bank or at the sea coast)
parole.testo: Originally a diminutive of мост (most, “bridge”) + -ик (-ik). The nautical meaning bridge is borrowed from Russian мо́стик (móstik).
Borrowed from Russian моше́нник (mošénnik), derived from Russian мошна́ (mošná, “sack, purse”) (Proto-Slavic *mošьna) + suffix -ик (-ik).

parole.significato: swindle, fraud, cheating (breaking of rules to gain advantage)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian моше́нничество (mošénničestvo). By surface analysis, моше́ник (mošénik) + -ство (-stvo).

parole.significato: museum (both as institution and as building)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian музе́й (muzéj), а transliteration of Ancient Greek μουσεῖον (mouseîon).
By surface analysis, на- (na-) + бяг (bjag, “run”). The sport meaning is borrowed from Russian набе́г (nabég).

parole.significato: draft, sketch (of a picture or text)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian набро́сок (nabrósok).

parole.significato: overhang, awning, lean-to (protrusion which protects from rain or sunlight)
parole.testo: Possibly borrowed from Russian на́вес (náves). By surface analysis, на- (na-) + вес (ves, “pending”) (equivalent to earlier *navěsъ).
Borrowed from Russian награ́да (nagráda), of vague origin. See etymology of Russian lemma for further discussion. Has displaced native Bulgarian мъзда́ (măzdá, “payment, award”) (obsolete).
Borrowed from Russian надме́нный (nadménnyj), itself derived from Proto-Slavic *nadъmenъ (“blown up”) + -ен (-en).

parole.significato: superstructure (a structure, storey, or part built above an existing building or base)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian надстро́йка (nadstrójka).
Borrowed from Russian намёк (namjók), with nativized pronunciation.
Borrowed from Russian наме́рение (namérenije). By surface analysis, наме́ря (namérja) + -ение (-enie).
Borrowed from Russian напряже́ние (naprjažénije). By surface analysis, напря́гам (naprjágam) + -ение (-enie).

parole.significato: plank bed (often used in prisons), bunk
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian на́ры (náry).

parole.significato: duty, detail, shift, watch, assignment (an assigned duty, especially military, police, guard, or service duty)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian наря́д (narjád).

Borrowed or mirrored from Russian насеко́мое (nasekómoje, “insect”), a calque of Latin īnsectum (“insected creature”). Technically a substantivized present passive participle of насе́ка (naséka, “to disect, to chop into pieces”) + -ом (-om) + -о (-o).

parole.significato: population (The people living within a political or geographical boundary)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian населе́ние (naselénije). By surface analysis, населя (naselja) + -ение (-enie). First attested in 1857.

parole.significato: tincture, concentrated liqueur/extract (beverage prepared by soaking materials in a solvent)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian насто́йка (nastójka). Synchronically, parseable as настоя́ (nastojá, “to press on”) + -ка (-ka).
Borrowed from Russian насто́льный (nastólʹnyj). By surface analysis, на- (na-) + стол (stol) + -ен (-en). Note that in Bulgarian стол (stol) means “chair”, not “table”, as in Russian.
Borrowed from Russian настоя́щий (nastojáščij). Synchronically, a present active participle of настоя́ (nastojá, “to stand by”).

parole.significato: setting, adjustment, configuration, setup, calibration, tuning, alignment (the act or result of adjusting, setting, con…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian настро́йка (nastrójka).
Influenced by Russian настро́йщик (nastrójščik), morphologically derived from настро́я (nastrója, “to set, to adjust”) + -чик (-čik).
Borrowed from Russian на́тиск (nátisk). Doublet of нати́сък (natísăk) (inherited form).
Borrowed from Russian национа́льный (nacionálʹnyj), from French nacional.
Borrowed from Russian нача́ло (načálo).

parole.significato: unaccounted expense or revenue (made expenditures that have not been formally recorded)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian начёт (načót), with a nativized pronunciation. By surface analysis, на- (na-) + чет (čet, “account”).

parole.significato: undertaking, enterprise, initiative (a task, action, or activity that has been begun with a particular purpose)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian начина́ние (načinánije).
Borrowed from Russian начина́я (načinája).
Borrowed from Russian неве́жа (nevéža). Displaced native неве́жда (nevéžda).
Borrowed from Russian невменя́емый (nevmenjájemyj). By surface analysis, не- (ne-, negating particle) + вменя́ем (vmenjáem, “sane”).
Borrowed from Russian невня́тный (nevnjátnyj). By surface analysis, не- (ne-, negating particle) + вня́тен (vnjáten, “articulate”).

Borrowed from Russian негодя́й (negodjáj), from Proto-Slavic *negodějь. Morphologically equivalent to негоду́вам (negodúvam, “to resent; to rebel, revolt”) + -яй (-jaj). Akin to Czech Nehodiv (shortened from an earlier *Nehodejevo) - a village in Bohemia.
Borrowed from Russian незаме́тный (nezamétnyj, “unnoticeable”).

parole.significato: firm, steadfast, unshakable, unwavering (stable, firm, and not able to be shaken or moved)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian незы́блемый (nezýblemyj).
Borrowed from Russian нелюди́мый (neljudímyj). By surface analysis, не- (ne-, negating particle) + лю́де (ljúde, “people”) + -им (-im).

parole.significato: not lethargic, not sluggish → prompt, expeditious, urgent
parole.testo: By surface analysis, не- (ne-, negating particle) + ме́длен (médlen, “lethargic, sluggish”), the later – a Russian borrowing.

Formally from не- (ne-) + обходи́м (obhodím, “bypassable”). The meaning is borrowed from Russian необходи́мый (neobxodímyj, “necessary”), a calque of German unumgänglich, via semantic shift not possible to bypass → necessary.
Borrowed from Russian необъя́тный (neobʺjátnyj). By surface analysis, не- (ne-, negating particle) + обя́тен (objáten, “encompassing”).
Borrowed from Russian неуда́ча (neudáča). By surface analysis, не- (ne-, negating particle) + уда́ча (udáča, “turnout”).

parole.significato: to overthrow, to depose, to cast down (to remove someone from power, rank, dignity, or a high position)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian низве́ргнуть (nizvérgnutʹ).
Borrowed from Russian но́мер (nómer). See there for more.
Borrowed from Russian нотариа́льный (notariálʹnyj).
Borrowed from Russian ну́жен (núžen). Displaced native нужден (nužden).

parole.significato: dressage (an equestrian discipline in which horse and rider perform controlled, precise movements)
parole.testo: Possibly, borrowed from Russian объе́здка (obʺjézdka).

parole.significato: volume, capacity (the amount of space occupied by a body or contained within something)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian объём (obʺjóm).

parole.significato: use, usage, circulation (practical use or general currency in speech, life, or society)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian обихо́д (obixód), from Proto-Slavic *obixodъ.

parole.significato: facing, coating (that covers the facade of something)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian облицо́вка (oblicóvka). By surface analysis, об- (ob-) + лице́ (licé, “face”) + -овка (-ovka).

parole.significato: fragment, piece, splinter, shard (a piece broken off from a larger object)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian обло́мок (oblómok).
Borrowed from Russian обобще́ние (obobščénije). By surface analysis, обобщя́ (obobštjá) + -ение (-enie).
Borrowed from Russian обобщи́ть (obobščítʹ).
Borrowed from Russian обо́з (obóz), from Proto-Slavic *obozъ. Cognate with Czech oboz and Polish obóz.
Borrowed from Russian обо́л (oból) or French obole, itself from Latin obolus, from Ancient Greek ὀβολός (obolós).
Borrowed from Russian огро́мный (ogrómnyj).
Borrowed from Russian олига́рх (oligárx) or German Oligarch, ultimately from Ancient Greek ὀλίγοι (olígoi, “few”) + ἀρχή (arkhḗ, “rule”).
Diachronically, borrowed from Russian опе́ка (opéka). Synchronically, an action noun of Etymology 1.
Borrowed from Russian опеку́н (opekún), from Proto-Slavic *opekunъ. By surface analysis, опе́ка (opéka) + -ун (-un).

parole.significato: omission, oversight, lapse (an involuntary failure to do something because of inattention, oversight, or negligence)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian опуще́ние (opuščénije), from опусти́ть (opustítʹ).
Borrowed from Russian о́рден (órden) through German Orden, from Latin ordō.
Borrowed from Russian ориента́ция (orijentácija), from French orientation.
Borrowed from Russian оса́нка (osánka).

parole.significato: to inform, to notify, to apprise
parole.testo: Likely borrowed from Russian осве́домить (osvédomitʹ).
Probably borrowed from Russian осо́ба (osóba) in the 19th century.
Borrowed from Russian отста́вка (otstávka).

parole.significato: pinworm (parasitic roundworm of genus Enterobius or more generally of family Oxyuridae)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian остри́ца (ostríca, “pinworm”), probably a calque of the scientific name for the family Oxyuridae. Morphologically equivalent to Etymology 1.

parole.significato: retreat signal (a military signal ordering troops to stop an action, withdraw, or cease an alarm or attack)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian отбо́й (otbój), from Proto-Slavic *otъbojь.

parole.significato: opening, hole, aperture, orifice (an open space or hole in a surface, wall, object, or structure)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian отве́рстие (otvérstije). Doublet of отвъ́рстие (otvắrstie).
Borrowed from Russian отвёртка (otvjórtka). Morphologically, equivalent to what would be native отвъ́ртам (otvắrtam, “to retort, to revolve”) + -ка (-ka).

parole.significato: rest (relief from exertion; state of quiet and recreation)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian о́тдых (ótdyx).

parole.significato: recoil, kickback (the backward movement of a firearm or weapon system caused by the force of firing)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian отка́т (otkát).
Borrowed from Russian отря́д (otrjád).
Borrowed from Russian отсу́тствие (otsútstvije).
Borrowed from Russian отте́нок (otténok), formally a diminutive of от- (ot-) + тен (ten, “shade”) (dated) + -ък (-ăk).
Borrowed from Russian отчёт (otčót), from Proto-Slavic *otъčьtъ.

parole.significato: desire, wish, inclination, willingness (inner readiness or desire to do something)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian охо́та (oxóta), from Proto-Slavic *oxota.

parole.significato: guarding, protection, security (the act or process of guarding, protecting, or securing someone or something)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian охра́на (oxrána).
Borrowed from Russian о́черк (óčerk).
Borrowed from Russian павильо́н (pavilʹón), from French pavillon. First attested in 1874.
Borrowed from Russian паке́т (pakét), in turn from German Paket and French paquet.
Either derivative of палата (palata) + -ка (-ka), or borrowed from Russian пала́тка (palátka).
Borrowed from Russian пала́ч (paláč), of unclear origin.
Borrowed from Russian парохо́д (paroxód).
Borrowed from Russian пега́нка (pegánka, “shelduck”).
Borrowed from Russian пе́мза (pémza).

parole.significato: five-year plan (for the national economy of the USSR)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian пятилетка (pjatiletka).
Borrowed from Russian пе́чка (péčka).
Borrowed from Russian пика (pika), from French pique.

parole.significato: pickup truck (truck with an open cargo bed)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian пика́п (pikáp), from English pickup.

Reanalyzed from an earlier пи́шен (píšen), itself borrowed from Russian пы́шный (pýšnyj, “fluffy, lush”). The form with -щ- is formed by hypercorrection or possibly confused for native пи́ща (píšta, “food, nourishment”) + -ен (-en).
Likely borrowed from Russian план (plan), possibly via Polish plan or German Plan, in turn from French plan, from Latin plānus.

parole.significato: club moss, lycopod (simple vascular spore plants of family Lycopodiales)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian плау́н (plaún). Doublet of плаву́н (plavún) (native term).
Borrowed from Russian пло́щадь (plóščadʹ). Morphologically formed as пло́сък (plósăk) + -яд (-jad).
The primary meaning is borrowed from Russian побо́рник (pobórnik), morphologically equivalent to побо́ря (pobórja, “to fight off, to wrestle”) + -ник (-nik)

parole.significato: pogrom, massacre (a violent attack, massacre, or organized persecution directed against an ethnic, religious, social, o…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian погро́м (pogróm).

parole.significato: lift, hoist, elevator (a machine or device for raising, lowering, or moving loads, vehicles, people, or materials verti…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian подъёмник (podʺjómnik). By surface analysis, поде́м (podém) + -ник (-nik).
Probably borrowed from Russian по́длый (pódlyj), ultimately from Proto-Slavic *podьlъ.
Possibly from Russian позиция (pozicija).
Borrowed from Russian поко́рнейший (pokórnejšij). Synchronically, a comparative degree of поко́рен (pokóren, “submissive”) + -ейш (-ejš).
Borrowed through Russian поли́тика (polítika) and Polish polityka, from Latin polīticus & Ancient Greek πολιτικός (politikós). First attested in 1855.
Borrowed from Russian поли́ция (polícija), borrowed from Polish policja, a learned borrowing from Late Latin polītīa, influenced by French police. First attested in 1848.
Borrowed from Russian полк (polk), ultimately of Germanic origin. At least partially, a doublet of пълк (pălk).

parole.significato: colonel (a commissioned officer in an armed military organization, typically the highest rank before flag officer ranks…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian полко́вник (polkóvnik). By surface analysis, полк (polk) + -овник (-ovnik). First attested in 1847. Cognate with Bulgarian пълк (pălk) and Bulgarian плък (plăk).

parole.significato: pole (either of the two points on the earth's surface around which it rotates)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian по́люс (póljus), from Latin polus, from Ancient Greek πόλος (pólos, “axis of rotation”).
Borrowed from Russian поля́к (polják), borrowed from Polish Polak.
Borrowed from Russian поры́в (porýv).

parole.significato: to spoil, to ruin (to destroy the value of something)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian по́ртить (pórtitʹ), ultimately from Proto-Slavic *pъrtiti.
Borrowed from Russian поря́док (porjádok), from Proto-Slavic *porędъkъ. Formally a resultant of поре́ждам (poréždam, “to arrange”) + -ък (-ăk).
Borrowed from Russian посо́л (posól).
Borrowed from Russian посо́льство (posólʹstvo), also analysed as посо́л (posól, “ambassador (dated)”) + -ство (-stvo).

parole.significato: having been stricken, having suffered an accident
parole.testo: Likely borrowed from Russian пострада́вший (postradávšij). Formally the past active participle of Bulgarian постра́дам (postrádam, “to suffer an accident”) + -авш (-avš).

parole.significato: tableware, dishes, crockery, dishware, utensils (vessels and utensils used for eating, drinking, serving, or preparing…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian посу́да (posúda), from Proto-Slavic *posǫda.

parole.significato: to confirm, to corroborate, to affirm (to state or write that something is true)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian подтвержда́ть (podtverždátʹ). By surface analysis, потвърдя́ (potvărdjá) + -вам (-vam).

parole.significato: descendant, offspring, issue (biological descendent of a person)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian пото́мок (potómok).
Likely borrowed from Russian потерпе́вший (poterpévšij). Formally а past active participle of Bulgarian потърпя́ (potărpjá, “to endure”) + -евш (-evš).

parole.significato: initiative, undertaking (an action or proposal begun by someone in order to start or achieve something)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian почи́н (počín).
Borrowed from Russian почти́ (počtí), an imperative of *počьsti whence native Bulgarian почета́ (početá, “to take into account”).
Borrowed from Russian по́шлый (póšlyj).

parole.significato: government (higher executive and administrative body of state governance)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian прави́тельство (pravítelʹstvo).
Borrowed from Russian предме́т (predmét) through Polish przedmiot, itself a calque of Latin obiectum.

parole.significato: provision, regulation, rule, prescription (mandatory requirement in a law, statute, regulation, etc.)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian предписа́ние (predpisánije). By surface analysis, предпи́ша (predpíša) + -ание (-anie).
Borrowed from Russian предпочита́ть (predpočitátʹ) and предпоче́сть (predpočéstʹ).

Borrowed from Russian предпочтение (predpočtenije), предпочтаньe (predpočtanʹe), or from предпочитан (predpočitan, “preferred”, past participle of предпочи́там (predpočítam)) + -ие (-ie, “deverbal suffix”).
Borrowed from Russian предпочте́ние (predpočténije).

Borrowed from Russian предсказу́емый (predskazújemyj), itself – of Church Slavonic origin. Synchronically, a fossilized present passive participle of предска́звам (predskázvam, “to foretell”) + -уем (-uem).
Borrowed from Russian президе́нт (prezidént), from German Präsident.
Borrowed from Russian преиспо́дняя (preispódnjaja).
Borrowed from Russian пре́лесть (prélestʹ) (Church Slavonic loanword), ultimately from Proto-Slavic *perlьstь (“allure”). Compare Old Church Slavonic прѣльсть (prělĭstĭ, “trickery, deceit, allure”).
Borrowed from Russian прецеде́нт (precedént), from Latin praecēdēns.
Borrowed from Russian прибо́р (pribór). First attested in 1871.

Probably borrowed or influenced by Russian придирчи́вый (pridirčívyj), ultimately a calque of Latin praetēnsus. Morphologically equivalent to приди́рям (pridírjam, “to stretch out; to pretend”) + -чив (-čiv).
Influenced by Russian приёмщик (prijómščik), morphologically derived from прие́мам (priémam, “to accept, receive”) + -чик (-čik).
Borrowed from Russian приключить (priključitʹ).
Borrowed from Russian приключить (priključitʹ). By surface analysis, при- (pri-) + ключ (ključ) + -вам (-vam)
Borrowed from Russian приме́р (primér).

parole.significato: annex, annexe, extension, addition, outbuilding (a part or small building added to the side of an existing building)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian пристро́йка (pristrójka).
Borrowed from Russian притесне́ние (pritesnénije, “oppression”).
Borrowed from Russian притесни́ть (pritesnítʹ, “to oppress”).
Borrowed from Russian причастие (pričastije), from Old Church Slavonic причѧстьѥ (pričęstĭje), a calque of Latin participium. By surface analysis, при- (pri-, “part”) + част (čast) + -ие (-ie).
Synchronically, a result noun of приче́ша (pričéša, “to comb”) + -ка (-ka). Diachronically, possibly borrowed from Russian причёска (pričóska) with a nativized pronunciation.

parole.significato: shelter, refuge, haven (a place where someone finds protection, safety, or rest)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian прию́т (prijút), from Proto-Slavic *prijǫtъ.
Borrowed from Russian прия́тный (prijátnyj).

parole.significato: to try, to attempt (to make an effort to do or accomplish something)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian про́бовать (próbovatʹ).

parole.significato: conductor (something that can transmit electricity, heat, light, or sound)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian проводни́к (provodník).
Borrowed from Russian провока́ция (provokácija), from Latin prōvocātiō.
Borrowed from Russian проклятье (prokljatʹje).

Borrowed from Russian промежу́ток (promežútok), formally identical to про- (pro-, “amidst, between”) + ме́жду (méždu) + -тък (-tăk). The final element is interpreted in Bulgarian as a suffix, but ultimately reflects the noun ток (tok, “current”).
Borrowed from Russian промы́шленный (promýšlennyj).

parole.significato: insight, penetration, perceptiveness (deep understanding of the essence, meaning, or inner nature of something)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian проникнове́ние (proniknovénije).

parole.significato: process (a series of natural, social, cognitive, or manufacturing events, changes, or operations)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian проце́сс (procéss), from Latin processus.

parole.significato: spring, coil spring (an elastic mechanical part that can be compressed, stretched, or bent and then return to its origi…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian пружи́на (pružína), from Proto-Slavic *prǫžina.

parole.significato: psychology (field of study of the mind)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian психоло́гия (psixológija). By surface analysis, психо- (psiho-) + -ло́гия (-lógija).

parole.significato: audience (group of people seeing a performance)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian пу́блика (públika), from Latin publicus.

parole.significato: tack button of an old-style garment (usually uniforms or mantles)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian пу́говица (púgovica), a diminutive form of an earlier *pǫgy (“knob”).

From obsolete Russian пудо́вка (pudóvka) with Bulgarianized stress; equivalent to пуд (pud) + -ов- (-ov-) + -ка (-ka). Note that for some reason the current Russian term for a kettlebell, ги́ря (gírja), is used in Bulgarian for a dumbbell.
Borrowed from Russian путеше́ственник (putešéstvennik).
Borrowed from Russian равнове́сие (ravnovésije).
Borrowed from Russian разбо́й (razbój), of Church Slavonic origin. Cognate with Romanian război.
Borrowed from Russian разви́тие (razvítije). By surface analysis, разви́я (razvíja, “to develop”) + -тие (-tie).

parole.significato: debauchery, dissoluteness, dissipation, licentiousness, profligacy, depravity, vice (morally corrupt, dissolute, or lic…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian развра́т (razvrát).

parole.significato: rout, disaster, debacle (a complete and severe defeat, especially in war, politics, sport, or competition)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian разгро́м (razgróm).

parole.significato: revelry, debauchery, dissipation, bender (careless and irresponsible spending of time in extravagance and excessive amu…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian разгу́л (razgúl).

parole.significato: ration list, food allocation (a calculated list or distribution of food products, portions, or ingredients)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian раскла́дка (raskládka).
By surface analysis, раз- (raz-, “apart”) + кол (kol). The religious sense is possibly borrowed from Russian раско́л (raskól). Cognate with Romanian răscol.
Borrowed from Russian разрабо́тчик (razrabótčik), morphologically equivalent to разрабо́тя (razrabótja, “to develop”) + -чик (-čik).

parole.significato: calculation, estimate, reckoning, computation (a calculated assessment of quantities, costs, needs, time, or expected r…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian расчёт (rasčót).

parole.significato: to be able to read, to decipher (something abstruse)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian рассчита́ть (rassčitátʹ).

parole.significato: shell (exoskeleton of mollusca, typically snails, rapana, mussels)
parole.testo: Formed from ра́ка (ráka, “old-style casket, chest”) (historical, outdated) + -овина (-ovina). At least the secondary meaning cavity, flaw (if not the word itself) is borrowed from Russian ра́ковина (rákovina).

parole.significato: frame (a rigid structure surrounding, supporting, or enclosing something)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian ра́ма (ráma, “frame”), from German Rahmen (“frame”).

parole.significato: whelk, sea snail (marine gastropod of family Muricidae)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian рапа́на (rapána), ultimately a derivative of Latin rāpum (“turnip”) due to the similarity of the creature to a turnip tuber.
Borrowed from Russian ре́вность (révnostʹ).
Borrowed from Russian реконстру́кция (rekonstrúkcija), from Latin reconstructio.
Borrowed from Russian ры́царь (rýcarʹ), from Middle High German ritter.
Borrowed from Russian ром (rom), from English rum or French rhum.
Borrowed from Russian ро́та (róta).
Borrowed from Russian рубе́ж (rubéž). By surface analysis, ръ́бя (rắbja, “to fringe”) + -еж (-ež). Doublet of ръбе́ж (răbéž) (dialectal inhereted term).
Borrowed from Russian ру́бка (rúbka), from Dutch roef.
Borrowed from Russian рубль (rublʹ).
Borrowed from Russian руготня́ (rugotnjá); equivalent to руга́я (rugája, “to swear, to curse”) + -атня́ (-atnjá). Akin to native Bulgarian ръгня́ (răgnjá, “proding”).

parole.significato: to scold, to rebuke, to malign, to curse
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian руга́ть (rugátʹ), which is a doublet of ръга́я (răgája) (inherited), ultimately from Proto-Slavic *rǫgati. Superficially also resembles Bulgarian ръ́гам (rắgam, “to prod”), however, their semantics don't match exactly.
Borrowed from Russian руле́тка (rulétka), itself from French roulette. Equivalent to рули́рам (rulíram) + -етка (-etka).

parole.significato: male Russian citizen, national (from any ethnie)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian россия́нин (rossijánin).

parole.significato: female Russian citizen, national (from any ethnie)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian россия́нка (rossijánka).
Borrowed from Russian ру́сло (rúslo). Morphologically equivalent to ру́ша (rúša, “to trample”) (dialectal) + -сло (-slo).

parole.significato: unit of length, equal to 7 feet
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian са́жень (sáženʹ), from Proto-Slavic *sęženь (n-stem).

parole.significato: table napkin, serviette (usually, but not exclusively paper)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian салфетка (salfetka).
Borrowed from Russian салю́т (saljút), or directly from French salut, from Latin salūs.
Borrowed from Russian саме́ц (saméc), ultimately from Proto-Slavic *samьcь.
Borrowed from Russian самова́р (samovár).
Influenced by Russian самолёт (samoljót, “aeroplane”). Morphologically, derived from само- (samo-, “self-”) + летя́ (letjá, “to fly”).

Borrowed from Russian свиде́тель (svidételʹ), formally an agent noun of the obsolete сведя (svedja, “to witness, to know”) + -тел (-tel) (in Russian, OCS -ѣ- sometimes transforms into -и-). Replaced the native Bulgarian сведок (svedok).
Borrowed from Russian свире́пый (svirépyj), from Proto-Slavic *sverěpъ
Borrowed from Russian свита (svita), ultimately from French suite. Formally, a doublet of сюи́та (sjuíta) (direct French borrowing, meaning “musical suite”)
Borrowed from Russian сво́лочь (svóločʹ), from Proto-Slavic *sъvolčь.
Borrowed from Russian свято́й (svjatój).

parole.significato: safe (box, usually made of metal, in which valuables can be locked for safekeeping)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian сейф (sejf), borrowed from English safe.

parole.significato: syntax (set of rules that govern how words are combined)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian си́нтаксис (síntaksis), from Ancient Greek σύνταξις (súntaxis, “arrangement, coordination”).
Borrowed from Russian си́речь (sírečʹ), from Old Church Slavonic си рѣчь (si rěčĭ, “that is”), from си (si, “this”) + рѣчь (rěčĭ, “speech, utterance”).
Borrowed from Russian сказу́емое (skazújemoje), itself a calque of Latin praedicātum.

parole.significato: to defile, to desecrate, to profane, to sully
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian скверни́ть (skvernítʹ). Doublet of скърня́ (skărnjá) (inherited from Proto-Slavic).

parole.significato: scorpion (member of the arachnid order Scorpiones)
parole.testo: Likely from Russian скорпио́н (skorpión), ultimately from Ancient Greek σκορπίος (skorpíos).
Borrowed from Russian скро́мный (skrómnyj), from Polish skromny, from Proto-Slavic *sъkromьnъ. Morphologically from скром (skrom, “restricted, bounded”) (dialectal) + -ен (-en).

parole.significato: to be bored, to pass time tediously
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian скуча́ть (skučátʹ), morphologically equivalent to скуч(ен) (skuč(en), “boring”) + -а́я (-ája).

parole.significato: swarthy, dusky (having a darker or brownish complexion)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian сму́глый (smúglyj), from Proto-Slavic *smǫglъ.
Borrowed from Russian смут (smut), cognate with Old Church Slavonic съмѫтъ (sŭmǫtŭ), ultimately derivative of мътя (mătja).
Borrowed from Russian смуще́ние (smuščénije). By surface analysis, смутя́ (smutjá, “to disturb”) + -ение (-enie).
Borrowed from Russian снаря́д (snarjád). Synchronically, parsable as с- (s-) + на- (na-) + ред (red).
Borrowed from Russian снаряже́ние (snarjažénije). By surface analysis, снаря́д (snarjád) + -ение (-enie).
Borrowed from Russian собы́тие (sobýtije).
Borrowed from Russian со́бственный (sóbstvennyj).
Borrowed from Russian со́бственник (sóbstvennik). By surface analysis, со́бствен (sóbstven) + -ик (-ik).

parole.significato: decline, drop, fall, decrease, reduction (a lowering or decrease in amount, level, value, intensity, or quantity)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian спад (spad), from Proto-Slavic *sъpadъ. By surface analysis, с- (s-) + па́д (pád)
Borrowed from Russian сплав (splav).
Borrowed from Russian спосо́бный (sposóbnyj), from Proto-Slavic *sъposobьnъ. By surface analysis, спо́соб (spósob, “manner, skill”) + -ен (-en).
Borrowed from Russian спринцо́вка (sprincóvka), from a German source, perhaps Spritze (“syringe; injection”).

Borrowed from Russian ста́вка (stávka, “stake, bet; rate, tariff, wage rate”), from Russian ста́вить (stávitʹ, “to set, to place”), ultimately from Proto-Slavic *stàviti. Compare also the older spellings ставкъ, стафка noted in Bulgarian dictionaries.

parole.significato: aluminum foil for wrapping e.g. food
parole.testo: Likely borrowed from Russian станиоль (staniolʹ), from German Stanniol - ultimately from Latin stannum. See there for further etymology.
Borrowed from Russian старе́йший (staréjšij). Synchronically, a comparative degree of стар (star, “old, mature”) + -ейш (-ejš).
Borrowed from Russian статья́ (statʹjá).

parole.significato: to connect, to join, to link, to coordinate, to align, to fit together, to match up (to bring two or more things, parts…
parole.testo: Possibly, borrowed from Russian стыковать (stykovatʹ, “to dock, to join, to connect”).

parole.significato: poetastering (the writing of inferior poetry, or the state of being of an inferior poet)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian стихоплётство (stixopljótstvo). By surface analysis, стихопле́т (stihoplét) + -ство (-stvo).
Borrowed from Russian стол (stol, “table”). Diachronically, from the same origin as the inherited term.
Borrowed from Russian столо́вая (stolóvaja).

parole.significato: aspiration, striving, endeavour, endeavor, pursuit, drive, ambition, desire, longing, yearning, urge, impulse (a strong…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian стремле́ние (stremlénije).
Borrowed from Russian стре́пет (strépet), probably related to Proto-Slavic *sterpьtiti (“to move suddenly, to trample”).

Borrowed from Russian суеве́рие (sujevérije), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic соуѥвѣрьѥ (sujevěrĭje). First attested in 1872. By surface analysis, суе- (sue-) + вя́ра (vjára) + -ие (-ie), literally, “superficial faith”.
Borrowed from Russian суета́ (sujetá).

parole.significato: scenario (outline or model of an expected or supposed sequence of events)
parole.testo: Possibly borrowed from Russian сцена́рий (scenárij), borrowed from German Szenario, borrowed from Italian scenario, from scena + -ario.

parole.significato: to consider, to deem, to regard
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian счи́тать (sčítatʹ), from Proto-Slavic *sъčitati (“to regard, to consider”). By surface analysis, с- (s-) + читам (čitam).

parole.significato: subbotnik (unpaid voluntary labor on a day off, usually Saturday, for a community or state project, common during the s…
parole.testo: Calque of Russian суббо́тник (subbótnik). By surface analysis, съ́бота (sắbota) + -ник (-nik).

Borrowed from Russian сооруже́ние (sooružénije) and subsequently relevelled to the phonetic patterns of Bulgarian (Russian -у- changed to Bulgarian -ъ- as a reflex of Proto-Slavic *-ǫ-). By surface analysis, съ- (să-) + oръ́дие (orắdie, “device, weapon”) + -ение (-enie).
Borrowed from Russian сочета́ние (sočetánije). By surface analysis, съчета́я (săčetája, “to combine”) + -ние (-nie, “deverbal noun-forming suffix”)

Borrowed from Russian сою́з (sojúz), itself borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съѭзъ (sŷjǫzŭ) - an alternative form of Old Church Slavonic съвѫзъ (sŭvǫzŭ). Cognate with the native dialectal terms Bulgarian въз m (văz), възе n (văze, “binder, fastener”), from Proto-Slavic *ǫzъ (“bond, tie”). The secon

parole.significato: salmon (one of several species of fish, typically of the Salmoninae subfamily, brownish above with silvery sides and de…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian сёмга (sjómga).
Borrowed from Russian таз (taz).
Borrowed from Russian тайга́ (tajgá).

parole.significato: curd cheese, tvorog (type of cheese popular in Eastern Europe)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian тваро́г (tvaróg) or Polish twaróg, morphologically equivalent to тва́ра (tvára, “curd”) (dialectal) + -ог (-og). Doublet of кварк (kvark) (German borrowing of Slavic origin).
Borrowed from Russian терза́ть (terzátʹ), from Proto-Slavic *tьrzati (“to pluck, to tear”). A doublet of natively inherited тъ́рзам (tắrzam).

parole.significato: leak, leakage (of a pipe or water)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian течь (tečʹ).
Borrowed from Russian тлен (tlen), from Proto-Slavic *tъlěnъ.

parole.significato: adds emphasize to the last entry in an enumeration: also, as well, likewise
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian тоже (tože), from Proto-Slavic *to že.
Borrowed from Russian то́чка (tóčka).
Borrowed from Russian то́чно (tóčno), from Russian то́чный (tóčnyj).
Borrowed from Russian транспорти́р (transportír), ultimately from Latin trānsportō.
Borrowed from Russian трево́га (trevóga), instead of expected тървога (tărvoga).

parole.significato: anxious, worried, troubled, uneasy, distressed (feeling worry, anxiety, fear, or inner unrest)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian трево́жный (trevóžnyj), from Proto-Slavic *trьvožьnъ. By surface analysis, трево́га (trevóga) + -ен (-en).
Borrowed from Russian тре́ска (tréska), from Proto-Slavic *trěska (“cod”).
Borrowed from Russian трофе́й (troféj), а transliteration of Latin trophaeum, from Ancient Greek τρόπαιον (trópaion, “sign of victory”).

parole.significato: shake, jolt, shock, tremor (a sudden shaking, jolting, or trembling movement)
parole.testo: Probably borrowed from Russian трус (trus), from Proto-Slavic *trǫsъ.

parole.significato: shanty town, ghetto, slum (poor and densely populated part of a city)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian трущо́ба (truščóba, “ticket”) (from труск (trusk, “bush”) + -оба (-oba)).
Borrowed from Russian ту́ндра (túndra), borrowed from Kildin Sami тӯндрэ (tūndre), from Proto-Samic *tuontër (“a kind of mountain in Lapland”).
Borrowed from Russian тожде́ственный (toždéstvennyj).

parole.significato: identity (the quality of being exactly the same)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian то́ждество (tóždestvo), itself derived from Old Church Slavonic тожде (tožde) / тъжде (tŭžde, “the same”).

parole.significato: pull, traction, draft (a pulling force or the force by which something is drawn, hauled, or moved)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian тя́га (tjága), from Proto-Slavic *tęga or *tęgъ.

Likely borrowed from Russian уважа́емый (uvažájemyj). Formally a present passive participle of a ja-conjugation verb (see Russian уважа́ть (uvažátʹ)), related to Bulgarian ува́жа (uváža, “to honour”) + -аем (-aem).
Borrowed from Russian угро́за (ugróza). By surface analysis, deverbal from угрозя́ (ugrozjá), ultimately from Proto-Slavic *groza.
Borrowed from Russian уда́рник (udárnik).

Borrowed from Russian удостовере́ние (udostoverénije) (a calque of Latin certificātum (“made certain”)); equivalent to удостоверя́ (udostoverjá, “to certify”) + -ние (-nie). Parallel to the native Bulgarian удостоверя́ване (udostoverjávane, “verification”).
Borrowed from Russian у́зкий (úzkij). Morphologically related to въз (văz, “binder”) (dialectal) + -ък (-ăk).
Borrowed from Russian ука́з (ukáz).

parole.significato: tendency, inclination, leaning, propensity (a tendency, disposition, or leaning toward something)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian укло́н (uklón). By surface analysis, у- (u-) + клон (klon).
Borrowed from Russian уме́стный (uméstnyj).
By surface analysis, упа́дам (upádam, “to decline”) + -ък (-ăk). Diachronically, probably borrowed from Russian упа́док (upádok).
Borrowed from Russian упова́ть (upovátʹ), from Proto-Slavic *upъvati.

parole.significato: point-blank, close range (a very short distance from which a shot is fired directly at a target)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian упо́р (upór).

Borrowed from Russian урожа́й (urožáj), from Proto-Slavic *uroďajь. Morphologically equivalent to Bulgarian уро́дя (uródja, “to give birth”) (dialectal) + -яй (-jaj). Identical with outdated native Bulgarian урожда́й (uroždáj, “brood”).

parole.significato: to establish, to determine, to ascertain, to find out
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian установи́ться (ustanovítʹsja). By surface analysis, у- (u-) + -становя́ (-stanovjá).

parole.significato: to establish, to set up, to institute
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian устана́вливать (ustanávlivatʹ). By surface analysis, установя́ (ustanovjá) + -вам (-vam).

parole.significato: zealous, eager, diligent, assiduous, studious, steady, patient, thorough, painstaking
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian усе́рдный (usérdnyj).
Borrowed from Russian утро́ба (utróba), from Proto-Slavic *ǫtroba. Synchronically analyzable as въ́тре (vắtre, “inside”) + -оба (-oba).
Borrowed from Russian участие (učastije).
Borrowed from Russian уча́сток (učástok). Morphologically from у- (u-) + ча́ст (část, “part”) + -ък (-ăk).

parole.significato: ushanka (type of Russian hat with ear-flaps)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian уша́нка (ušánka), from уши (uši, “ears”) + -анка (-anka).

parole.significato: harm, damage, detriment, prejudice (harm, damage, or impairment caused to someone’s interests, rights, reputation, or p…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian ущерб (uščerb).

parole.significato: fiction, fantasy, science fiction (genre of literature, film, or art)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian фанта́стика (fantástika).
Borrowed from Russian физзаря́дка (fizzarjádka), clipped form of физи́ческая заря́дка (fizíčeskaja zarjádka) (“physical exercise, calisthenics”).
Likely from Russian физи́к (fizík).
Borrowed from Russian финансы (finansy), borrowed from French finance.
Borrowed from Russian финансовый (finansovyj), from финансы (finansy) + -овый (-ovyj). By surface analysis, финанси (finansi) + -ов (-ov).
Borrowed from Russian финтифлю́шка (fintifljúška). Further origin uncertain - hypotheses include derivation from Italian or German. Compare Polish fintifluszka.

Standardized colloquial form of an earlier ха́лостен (hálosten), derived from Russian холосто́й (xolostój, “idle, blank”). The native pronunciation has been probably levelled to resemble inherited ха́лост (hálost, “vanity, futility”). In Russian, the stress is on the suffix (rather than on the root)
Possibly from Russian хирурги́я (xirurgíja), or from хиру́рг (hirúrg) + -ия (-ija).
Borrowed from Russian хомяк (xomjak), probably influenced by an Iranian language (cf. Avestan 𐬵𐬀𐬨𐬀𐬉𐬯𐬙𐬀𐬭 (hamaēstar, “pest, one who makes mess”)).
Borrowed from Russian хребе́т (xrebét). Doublet of хръбе́т (hrăbét), obsolete form of Proto-Slavic *xrьbьtъ (“back”).
Borrowed from Russian хрип (xrip).
Borrowed from Russian ча́йник (čájnik).
Borrowed from Russian часть (častʹ), from Proto-Slavic *čęstь. Partially displaced native дял (djal).
Borrowed from Russian че́реп (čérep).
Borrowed from Russian чи́нный (čínnyj).
Borrowed from Russian чистка (čistka).

parole.significato: devil, demon, fiend (an evil supernatural being; the Devil)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian чёрт (čort), from Proto-Slavic *čьrtъ.

parole.significato: effigy, dummy (a figure of a person made of straw, rags, or similar material)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian чу́чело (čúčelo), from Proto-Slavic *čučelo.

parole.significato: gang of rogues, band of bandits
parole.testo: Reborrowed from Russian ша́йка (šájka), from Ottoman Turkish شایقه (şayka), from Bulgarian ша́йка (šájka, “saic”).

parole.significato: greatcoat (usually as a part of a uniform)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian шине́ль (šinélʹ), from French chenille.
Borrowed from Russian шо́мпол (šómpol), from Polish sztępel, from German Stempel.

parole.significato: happiness (the emotion of being happy; joy; elation)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian сча́стье (sčástʹje). By surface analysis, с- (s-, “part, lot”) + част (čast) + -ие (-ie).
Borrowed from Russian счастли́вый (sčastlívyj).

parole.significato: sensitive, delicate, touchy (requiring tact, caution, or careful handling)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian щекотли́вый (ščekotlívyj).

parole.significato: bayonet (a dagger mountable on a rifle or another firearm)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian штык (štyk), ultimately of Germanic origin. Doublet of щека (šteka) and стик (stik).
From Russian штурмово́й (šturmovój).

parole.significato: jeweler, jeweller (a person whose job is making, repairing or selling jewelry)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Russian ювели́р (juvelír), in turn from Dutch juwelier or German Juwelier.
Borrowed from Russian ю́нкер (júnker), in turn from German Junker.
Borrowed from Russian юфть (juftʹ).

parole.significato: safe house, rendezvous point (a secret place used for contact, meetings, hiding, or communication, especially in clande…
